query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) at high temperatures the dominant carrier of plasticity shifts from thermally activated screw dislocations to edge dislocations whose motion, strongly impeded by lattice distortions from chemical disorder, leads to a plateau in yield strength and subdued thermoelastic softening.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, single‐phase BCC refractory HEA (for example, NbTaHfTiZrV0.5) with well‐characterized chemical disorder and high lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying modification (or tailor processing) designed to alter local lattice distortion and hence the mobility of edge dislocations—for instance, adding a small fraction of an element that decreases the local misfit strain.
generation.conditions: Perform high-temperature tensile and creep tests across 673 K to 1073 K at controlled strain rates while conducting in situ neutron diffraction and TEM to monitor dislocation types and thermoelastic response.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions arising from chemical disorder that create heterogeneous energy barriers, promoting thermal super‐jog formation on edge dislocations.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures, screw dislocations govern plasticity; however, with increasing temperature thermal activation renders edge dislocations mobile. In the presence of high lattice distortion, these edge dislocations form super‐jogs that act as effective barriers to further glide, stabilizing the flow stress and leading to the observed yield strength plateau as well as minimal changes in elastic moduli with temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: In the baseline HEA, a pronounced high-temperature strength plateau and constrained elastic modulus variation are expected. If the intervention reduces the barrier for edge dislocation motion (by reducing local lattice distortion), the yield strength at high temperatures will show a more conventional decline with temperature and the thermoelastic properties will change accordingly.
generation.baseline: The standard NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 HEA tested under identical thermal and strain-rate conditions showing the yield strength plateau from approximately 673 K to 1073 K.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to apply primarily to homogeneous, fully solution‐hardened, single‐phase BCC refractory HEAs within a temperature regime where diffusion effects do not dominate the deformation process (i.e. below the onset of diffusion-controlled creep).
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from studies (e.g., PMC10453588 and PMC8446014) indicate an edge dislocation–dominated mechanism at elevated temperatures, it remains uncertain if edge dislocation super‐jogging is solely responsible for the plateau, given potential concurrent effects from grain boundary behavior or short-range ordering. This hypothesis extends previous findings on yield strength plateaus and edge dislocation effects by linking them directly to thermoelastic behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: (a) baseline NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 and (b) a modified alloy with a minor alloying addition intended to reduce lattice distortion (and hence alter edge dislocation behavior). Conduct high-temperature tensile and creep tests (673–1073 K) under controlled strain rates and perform in situ TEM and neutron diffraction analyses to identify dislocation character.
measurements: In situ observation and quantification of edge versus screw dislocation populations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy modified to reduce lattice distortions still exhibits a similar yield strength plateau and comparable edge dislocation activity as the baseline, or if thermoelastic properties fail to change as predicted, then the hypothesis that edge dislocation–mediated super‐jogging is responsible for high-temperature strength retention is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, the mechanical properties of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA were tested at elevated temperatures. Additionally, XRD, SEM, and TEM were used to thoroughly characterize the samples both before and after testing. The results are summarized below: Over a wide temperature range of RT-1223 K, the studied alloy exhibited excellent tensile mechanical properties. From RT to 678 K, the strength of the alloy was maintained above 1000 MPa; At 878–1078 K, the strength variation was small and no less than 800 MPa, and it nearly exceeded most commercial alloys. Coupled with an excellent cold workability, the alloy has the potential to be used as a new generation of high-temperature materials for the preparation of high-temperature-resistant parts in aerospace. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions showed similar trends at temperatures between 873 K and 1073 K. That is, a work hardening occurred after yielding, and then a gradual softening until fracture. The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures. Single-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) show remarkable mechanical properties, such as their high yield strength and substantial softening resistance at elevated temperatures. Hence, the in-depth study of the deformation behavior for body-centered cubic (BCC) refractory HEAs is a critical issue to explore the uncovered/unique deformation mechanisms. We have investigated the elastic and plastic deformation behaviors of a single BCC NbTaTiV refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using integrated experimental efforts and theoretical calculations. The in situ neutron diffraction results reveal a temperature-dependent elastic anisotropic deformation behavior. The single-crystal elastic moduli and macroscopic Young’s, shear, and bulk moduli were determined from the in situ neutron diffraction, showing great agreement with first-principles calculations, machine learning, and resonant ultrasound spectroscopy results. AbstractEnergy efficiency is motivating the search for new high-temperature (high-T) metals. Some new body-centered-cubic (BCC) random multicomponent “high-entropy alloys (HEAs)” based on refractory elements (Cr-Mo-Nb-Ta-V-W-Hf-Ti-Zr) possess exceptional strengths at high temperatures but the physical origins of this outstanding behavior are not known. Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations. This finding is surprising because plastic flows in BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys are generally controlled by screw dislocations.
